usage: the all-purpose 존댓말 thanks to anyone
반말, to a close friend or someone younger
격식, public, written, or to a customer
examples: 감사합니다.
Thank you.
the bare safe thanks you can say to anyone in any situation
도와주셔서 감사합니다.
Thank you for helping me.
attach ~아/어 주셔서 before 감사합니다 to thank for a specific action
A: 바쁘신데 시간 내 주셔서 정말 감사합니다. / B: 별말씀을요, 당연히 해야죠.
A: Thank you so much for making time despite being so busy. / B: Not at all, of course I would.
full polite exchange after someone goes out of their way; note the humble reply 별말씀을요
nuance: 감사합니다 is the default 존댓말 'thank you' safe with literally anyone — a stranger, a clerk, a teacher, your boss — and never wrong. It comes from Sino-Korean 감사(感謝), giving it a slightly formal, composed feel compared to the warmer native alternative 고맙습니다. The formality ladder runs: 고마워 (반말, friends/juniors) → 고마워요 (gentle polite) → 감사합니다 (standard polite) → 대단히 감사합니다 / 감사드립니다 (격식, speeches, written). The nearest alternative is 고맙습니다, which is pure native Korean and sounds a touch warmer and more personal; both are equally polite, and the choice is mostly about tone rather than rank. The classic English-speaker error is stacking a noun directly: you cannot say '도움 감사합니다' as if words simply pile up — to thank for an action you must attach ~아/어 주셔서 (도와주셔서 감사합니다). Another mistake is using 고마워 with strangers or anyone older, which sounds presumptuous and rude.

structuredNuance.t: 감사합니다 is the default 존댓말 'thank you' safe with literally anyone — a stranger, a clerk, a teacher, your boss — and never wrong. It comes from Sino-Korean 감사(感謝), giving it a slightly formal, composed feel compared to the native alternative 고맙습니다.

Formality ladder: 고마워 (반말, friends/juniors) → 고마워요 (gentle polite) → 감사합니다 (standard polite) → 대단히 감사합니다 / 감사드립니다 (격식, speeches, written). 감사드립니다 uses the humble auxiliary 드리다 and is the most deferential spoken form.
Nearest alternative is 고맙습니다 — pure native Korean, equally polite, and a touch warmer. The dividing line is tone and origin, not rank. Use 고맙습니다 when you want sincerity over formality.
To thank for a specific action, insert ~아/어 주셔서: 도와주셔서 감사합니다, 기다려 주셔서 감사합니다. To amplify, add 정말/너무/대단히 before 감사합니다.

English speakers try to thank for a noun by stacking it directly ('도움 감사합니다') — Korean needs the favor connector ~아/어 주셔서. Also, overusing 고마워 with strangers or seniors is a common register mistake; it is 반말 and sounds rude to anyone you are not already close with.

mistakes: Saying 고마워 to a stranger, clerk, or anyone older — that is 반말 and sounds rude; default to 감사합니다 or at least 고마워요.
Trying to thank for an action by just naming it ('도와 감사합니다') — Korean needs ~아/어 주셔서: 도와주셔서 감사합니다.
Writing 감사 합니다 with a space — 감사합니다 is one word; the space is wrong.

usage: 반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
softer polite, to a peer or familiar adult
examples: 고맙습니다.
Thank you.
the warm native-Korean polite thanks; safe with anyone
챙겨 줘서 고마워.
Thanks for looking out for me.
반말 with ~아/어 줘서 between close friends; the ㅂ-irregular is 고마워, never 고맙어
A: 걱정 많이 했는데 잘 됐다니 다행이에요. / B: 이렇게까지 신경 써 주시고, 정말 고맙습니다.
A: I was worried, but I'm glad it worked out. / B: Thank you so much for caring this much about me.
A/B exchange showing 고맙습니다 in heartfelt context, not just a ritual reply
nuance: 고맙습니다 is the native-Korean twin of 감사합니다 and is equally polite — many Koreans feel it sounds warmer and more personal, while 감사합니다 has a slightly formal, Sino-Korean edge. You say it to anyone in 존댓말; drop to 고마워요 (gently polite) or 고마워 (반말) as closeness rises and age or rank falls. The dividing line versus 감사합니다 is feel and origin (native vs Sino-Korean), NOT politeness level — 고맙습니다 is never 'less polite'. The verb 고맙다 is a ㅂ-irregular: polite ending → 고맙습니다 (formal polite with ㅂ kept before consonant), casual polite → 고마워요, 반말 → 고마워 (ㅂ softens to 워 before vowel). Never say 고맙어 — that is the most common conjugation error for English speakers. A second pitfall is defaulting to 감사합니다 in every context; sprinkling 고맙습니다 with people you know sounds more human and emotionally genuine.

structuredNuance.t: 고맙습니다 is the native-Korean twin of 감사합니다 and is equally polite — many Koreans feel it sounds warmer and more personal, while 감사합니다 has a slightly formal, Sino-Korean edge. Use it to anyone in 존댓말; drop register as closeness rises.
고마워 (반말, friends/juniors) → 고마워요 (gently polite) → 고맙습니다 (standard polite) → 참 고맙습니다 (more heartfelt). The 반말 form 고마워 is only for people you are already close with.
The dividing line versus 감사합니다 is feel and origin (native vs Sino-Korean), NOT politeness level. 고맙습니다 sounds more personal and heartfelt; 감사합니다 sounds more standard and composed.
ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 고맙다 → 고맙습니다 (formal polite, ㅂ before consonant) / 고마워요 (casual polite, ㅂ→워 before vowel) / 고마워 (반말). Never 고맙어 — that ignores the ㅂ-irregular rule.
English speakers conjugate 반말 as 고맙어 — but 고맙다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it must be 고마워. A second trap is always reaching for 감사합니다; Koreans find 고맙습니다 warmer and more heartfelt in personal contexts.

mistakes: Conjugating 반말 as 고맙어 — 고맙다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 고마워, never 고맙어.
Assuming 고맙습니다 is less polite than 감사합니다 and avoiding it with seniors — both are fully polite; the difference is warmth, not rank.
Saying 고마워요 to your boss in a formal setting — prefer 고맙습니다 or 감사합니다; 고마워요 can feel a touch too casual upward.

usage: polite reply to thanks; slightly formal/old-fashioned
반말, brushing off a friend's thanks
the natural everyday reply people actually use
examples: A: 감사합니다. / B: 천만에요.
A: Thank you. / B: You're welcome.
the textbook A/B reply, correct but slightly formal-sounding in daily life
고마워요. — 천만에요, 도움이 됐다니 다행이에요.
Thank you. — You're welcome; I'm glad it helped.
softening 천만에요 with a follow-up clause so it doesn't sound stiff
덕분에 잘 끝냈어요. — 천만에요, 별것도 아닌데요.
Thanks to you it went well. — You're welcome, it was really nothing.
pairing with 별것 아니에요 for a humble, natural close
nuance: 천만에요 is the textbook 'you're welcome' reply to 감사합니다, but in real daily life it sounds a little formal or even old-fashioned to younger Koreans, so people more often say 아니에요, 별말씀을요, or 별거 아니에요 to wave off thanks. The literal phrase means '(that's) ten thousand and more (words of thanks)' — i.e. 'far from it, not at all'. The formality ladder: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 / 별거 아니에요 (everyday polite) → 천만에요 (polite, slight vintage feel) → 천만의 말씀입니다 (격식, very humble). The dividing line versus 별말씀을요 is tone: 별말씀을요 is humble and flows naturally upward when a senior thanks you, while 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook and can sound a touch awkward. The key English-speaker mistake is treating 천만에요 like the constant, reflexive 'you're welcome' of English — Koreans often reply to thanks with a smile, 네, or 아니에요, and over-firing 천만에요 sounds stilted and overly formal.

structuredNuance.t: 천만에요 literally means 'ten thousand and more (words)' — i.e. '(there are) ten million [thanks to give back]; not at all.' The real function is deflecting thanks politely. The archaic feel comes from 천만(千萬) 'ten million', an idiom of rhetorical excess meaning 'far from it'.
Formality ladder: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 / 별거 아니에요 (everyday polite) → 천만에요 (polite, slightly vintage) → 천만의 말씀입니다 (격식, very humble). Use 아니에요 in most everyday situations — it's warmer and less dated.

The dividing line versus 별말씀을요: 별말씀을요 is humble and flows naturally upward (when a senior or customer thanks you), while 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook and can sound slightly stiff. In daily life, 아니에요 or 별말씀을요 sounds more genuine.

Soften by adding a follow-up clause: 천만에요, 도움이 됐다니 다행이에요. To intensify or write formally: 천만의 말씀입니다. To wave off thanks in 반말: 뭘, 뭘 그런 걸. Never say 천만이에요 — the fixed form is 천만에요, not a copula construction.

English speakers fire 천만에요 reflexively after every thanks, like 'you're welcome' — it sounds stilted. Koreans often reply with 네 + a nod, or 아니에요 in daily life. Reserve 천만에요 for slightly formal moments.

mistakes: Using 천만에요 reflexively after every thanks like English 'you're welcome' — it sounds stiff; 아니에요 or 별말씀을요 is more natural.
Saying 천만에요 to a close friend — too formal; use 뭘 or 아니야 in 반말.
Misspelling it 천만애요 — it is 천만에요 (에, not 애).

english: Don't mention it. / Not at all.
usage: humble polite reply, often upward to a senior/customer
반말-ish casual shortening among close people
you're too kind to say so (formal)
격식, very humble deflection of praise/thanks
examples: A: 정말 도움이 많이 됐습니다. / B: 별말씀을요.
A: You were a real help. / B: Don't mention it.
humble deflection when someone above you thanks you
덕분에 큰 도움 받았습니다. — 별말씀을요.
You were a huge help. — Please, don't mention it.
deflecting a senior's thanks modestly in the workplace
바쁘신데 직접 와 주셔서 감사합니다. — 별말씀을요, 당연히 와야죠.
Thank you for coming in person despite being busy. — Not at all, of course I'd come.
pairing with 당연히 ~죠 to sound gracious and unforced
nuance: 별말씀을요 is a humble, polite way to wave off thanks or praise — literally '(what) unusual words (you say)' — meaning 'you needn't say such a thing; it was nothing'. It is the go-to when someone above you (a customer, a senior, an elder) thanks you and you want to sound genuinely modest, not just polite. The 말씀 is the honorific word for 'words/speech', so the phrase already raises the SPEAKER — making it naturally respectful upward. The formality ladder: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 (everyday polite) → 별말씀을요 (humble-polite, upward) → 별말씀을 다 하십니다 (격식). The dividing line versus 천만에요 is that 천만에요 is neutral-textbook, while 별말씀을요 leans 'I'm too humble to accept this praise' and works especially well toward seniors and customers. English speakers often mis-segment it as '별 말씀 이요' with spaces — it is a single set phrase 별말씀을요, where 을요 is the object marker + softening particle. Also, do not use it to a close friend — it is too formal; say 뭘 or 아니야.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '(what) unusual/extra words (you say)' — i.e. 'you needn't say such a thing; it was nothing'. The 말씀 is the honorific for 'words/speech', which already makes the phrase deferential by design.
Formality: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 (everyday) → 별말씀을요 (humble-polite, flows upward) → 별말씀을 다 하십니다 (격식). Best used when a senior or customer thanks you; sounds too formal to a close friend.

The dividing line versus 천만에요 is humility and direction: 별말씀을요 leans 'I'm too humble to accept this thanks' and flows naturally upward; 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook and slightly vintage. 별말씀을요 is the safer choice when a superior or customer thanks you.

Extend with a follow-up: 별말씀을요, 당연히 해야죠 / 별말씀을요, 저도 배운 게 많았습니다. To soften, prepend 아니에요: 아니에요, 별말씀을요. Very formal written or spoken escalation: 별말씀을 다 하십니다. In 반말 among friends the phrase shrinks to 별말을 — but that sounds odd in formal contexts.

English speakers mis-segment it as '별 말씀 이요' with spaces — it is the set phrase 별말씀을요. Also, using it with a close friend sounds overly formal; say 뭘 or 아니야 instead. Do not confuse 을요 here with the topic marker — it is object + softening particle.

mistakes: Using 별말씀을요 with a close friend — it is humble/formal; in 반말 just say 뭘 or 아니야.
Breaking it into 별 말씀 with a space or writing 별말씀이요 — the set phrase is 별말씀을요.
Thinking it only answers thanks — it also gracefully deflects praise ('you flatter me').

usage: the safe 존댓말 apology to anyone, esp. seniors/strangers
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
examples: 죄송합니다.
I'm sorry.
the bare polite apology, safe with anyone you don't know well
늦어서 죄송합니다.
I'm sorry I'm late.
reason + 아/어서 + 죄송합니다; the standard structure for apologizing for a cause
A: 제 실수로 불편을 드렸습니다. 정말 죄송합니다. / B: 아니에요, 괜찮아요.
A: I caused inconvenience because of my mistake. I'm truly sorry. / B: No, it's all right.
formal exchange owning the fault clearly; notice how 불편을 드리다 (cause inconvenience upward) pairs naturally
nuance: 죄송합니다 is the higher-deference 'I'm sorry', from Sino-Korean 죄송(罪悚), literally 'I feel I have committed a fault and am fearful before you'. That deferential weight makes it the correct apology toward strangers, seniors, customers, and your boss — situations where showing you lower yourself is required. The formality ladder: 미안해 (반말, peers/friends) → 미안해요 (gentle polite) → 죄송해요 / 죄송합니다 (polite, upward-safe) → 대단히 죄송합니다 / 죄송스럽습니다 (격식, serious fault). The dividing line versus 미안하다 is deference: 죄송하다 lowers yourself and is always safe upward; 미안하다 is more horizontal and personal, and sounds too casual to a boss. Three concrete English-speaker mistakes: (1) attaching the reason wrong — use X-아/어서 죄송합니다 (늦어서 죄송합니다), not '늦은 것 죄송'; (2) using 미안해 to a boss or stranger; (3) confusing it with 실례합니다, which is 'excuse me' for a small intrusion, not an apology for fault.

structuredNuance.t: From Sino-Korean 죄송(罪悚), literally 'I feel I have committed a fault and am fearful/ashamed before you'. The real function is a deferential apology that lowers the speaker — stronger and more formal than 미안합니다.
Formality: 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gentle polite) → 죄송해요 / 죄송합니다 (polite, upward-safe) → 대단히 죄송합니다 / 죄송스럽습니다 (격식). Use 죄송합니다 as your default to strangers, seniors, and customers.

Key dividing line versus 미안하다: 죄송하다 lowers yourself and is always safe upward; 미안하다 is more horizontal/personal. Using 미안해요 to a boss sounds under-deferential; using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds oddly stiff.
Add the reason with ~아/어서: 늦어서 죄송합니다, 잘못해서 죄송합니다. Intensify: 정말 / 대단히 죄송합니다. Very formal written form: 심심(深深)한 사과를 드립니다.

Three traps: (1) attach reason with ~아/어서, not a noun — '늦은 것 죄송' is wrong; say 늦어서 죄송합니다. (2) Never use 미안해 to a boss or stranger — it's 반말. (3) Do not swap in 실례합니다 for a real fault — 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a small intrusion, not an apology.

mistakes: Saying 미안해 to a boss, teacher, or stranger — that is 반말; use 죄송합니다 (or at least 미안해요) for a real apology upward.
Forming the reason wrong, e.g. '늦은 거 죄송' — use the ~아/어서 connector: 늦어서 죄송합니다.
Swapping in 실례합니다 to apologize for a real mistake — 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor intrusion, not an apology for fault.

usage: 존댓말 to a peer or familiar adult; warm, personal
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, neutral and a bit firmer
natural extension adding sincerity in 반말
examples: 미안해요.
I'm sorry.
a soft, personal polite apology to someone familiar or at peer level
연락 늦어서 미안해.
Sorry for the late reply.
everyday 반말 apology with ~아/어서 to a friend; note 연락 (contact) + 늦어서
A: 약속을 못 지켰네. 정말 미안해. / B: 아니야, 괜찮아. 다음에 보면 되지.
A: I couldn't keep my promise. I'm really sorry. / B: No, it's fine. We'll see each other next time.
반말 exchange showing authentic apology and warm reassurance between friends
nuance: 미안해요/미안하다 is the warmer, more horizontal 'sorry' — used downward or sideways: to friends, peers, your kids, or people close in age and rank. From Sino-Korean 미안(未安), literally 'not at ease (in my heart)', it expresses personal guilt rather than formal deference. The register ladder: 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gently polite) → 미안합니다 (firmer polite) → 죄송합니다 (deferential, upward/격식). The key dividing line versus 죄송하다 is deference: 미안하다 does NOT lower you toward the listener, so it can feel too casual or even presumptuous with a boss or customer — for those situations always choose 죄송합니다. English speakers wrongly treat 미안해요 and 죄송합니다 as interchangeable 'sorry'; using 미안해요 to your boss sounds insufficiently deferential, while using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds coldly distant. Also: the small 'sorry, excuse me' to squeeze past a stranger on the street is NOT 미안해요 but 실례합니다 / 잠시만요.

structuredNuance.t: From 미안(未安), literally 'not at ease in my heart'. The real meaning is personal guilt or regret — not the formal deference of 죄송합니다. This makes it warmer but less deferential.

Register ladder: 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gently polite, peer level) → 미안합니다 (firmer polite) → 죄송합니다 (deferential, upward). Use 미안해요 with peers and familiar adults; switch up to 죄송합니다 with bosses, strangers, and customers.

The key dividing line versus 죄송하다: 미안하다 does NOT lower you toward the listener; it expresses personal guilt at peer level. Using 미안해요 to a boss sounds under-deferential; using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds stiff.
Attach reason with ~아/어서: 연락 늦어서 미안해, 잊어버려서 미안해요. Intensify: 정말 미안해 / 너무 미안해. To apologize repeatedly or dramatically: 미안하고 미안해.

English speakers treat 미안해요 and 죄송합니다 as interchangeable — they are not. Also, don't use 미안해요 to squeeze past someone in a crowd; that's 실례합니다 or 잠시만요. And never say 미안해 to someone you just met — too intimate.

mistakes: Using 미안해요 to a boss, customer, or elder for a real fault — it isn't deferential enough; say 죄송합니다.
Using 미안하다 to brush past someone in a crowd — Koreans say 실례합니다 or 잠시만요, not 미안해요, for that.
Saying 미안해 to someone you've just met — too familiar; with strangers use 미안합니다/죄송합니다.

english: It's okay. / That's all right. / No, thank you.
usage: polite; reassuring, accepting an apology, or politely declining
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, firmer and more neutral
yes, it's fine / no, I'm okay
natural extension; context tells accept vs decline
examples: A: 죄송해요. / B: 괜찮아요, 그럴 수도 있죠.
A: I'm sorry. / B: It's okay, these things happen.
accepting an apology graciously; 그럴 수도 있죠 adds warmth
한 잔 더 드릴까요? — 아니요, 괜찮아요. 잘 마셨습니다.
Shall I pour you another? — No, I'm fine, thank you. I've had plenty.
괜찮아요 as a polite DECLINE — this is the triple-meaning trap
많이 다치셨어요? — 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 걱정 마세요.
Are you badly hurt? — No, I'm all right. Don't worry.
괜찮아요 reassuring someone about your own physical state
nuance: 괜찮아요 does triple duty: 'it's okay / don't worry about it' (accepting an apology or reassuring), 'I'm fine' (about your own state or health), and crucially 'no, thank you' (politely declining an offer). The word traces back to 괜찮다, a contracted form of 관계없다 (關係없다) — literally 'there is no relationship/connection (to worry about)', i.e. 'it doesn't matter'. That origin explains why all three uses share the idea that the matter has no hold over you. The decline meaning trips English speakers most, because English 'okay' or 'fine' to an offer usually signals acceptance — but 괜찮아요 to a Korean host's offer means you are turning it DOWN. To accept, you must clearly say 네, 주세요 / 네, 부탁드립니다. Register: 괜찮아 (반말) → 괜찮아요 (polite) → 괜찮습니다 (firmer/격식). The nearest relatives are 됐어요 (also 'I'm good/no need', but sharper and can sound curt or dismissive) and 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing', used mainly to deflect apologies). 괜찮아요 is the softest and most versatile of the three.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮다 is a contracted form of 관계없다 (關係없다), literally 'there is no relationship/connection (to worry about)'. From this 'it doesn't matter' root, the word branches into three real uses: accepting apologies, stating you are fine, and declining offers. All three share the idea that the matter has no hold over you.
괜찮아 (반말, friends/juniors) → 괜찮아요 (polite, most common) → 괜찮습니다 (firmer/격식). Keep 괜찮아 for people you are close with; use 괜찮아요 or 괜찮습니다 with strangers and seniors.

Nearest relatives: 됐어요 (also 'no need / I'm done', but can sound curt or even annoyed); 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing', for deflecting apologies). 괜찮아요 is the softest and most versatile of the three. Choose 됐어요 only when you want finality, not just reassurance.
To soften a decline: 아, 괜찮아요 / 정말 괜찮아요. To reassure: 걱정 마세요, 괜찮아요. To check on someone: 괜찮으세요? (question, honorific form). Never say 괜찮어 — the stem is 괜찮다, so polite is 괜찮아요 (아-ending, not 어).

When a host offers food or a refill and you say 괜찮아요, you are turning it DOWN, not accepting. To accept, say 네, 주세요. Also, 됐어요 (an alternative decline) can sound blunt or even annoyed — 괜찮아요 is always gentler for refusals.

mistakes: Answering an offer of food/drink with 괜찮아요 expecting MORE — it means 'no, I'm fine'; to accept, say 네, 주세요.
Using 괜찮아 with a stranger or senior — that is 반말; say 괜찮아요/괜찮습니다.
Confusing 괜찮아요 with 됐어요 in tone — 됐어요 can sound blunt/annoyed; 괜찮아요 stays gentle.

usage: 존댓말 to get attention, pass by, or interrupt a stranger
clipped/반말-ish, only among close people or muttered
격식, before entering or doing something intrusive
natural extension; 저 softens the approach
examples: 실례합니다, 화장실이 어디예요?
Excuse me, where's the restroom?
standard opener before asking a stranger a question; notice 실례합니다 comes FIRST
A: 실례합니다, 잠깐 지나가도 될까요? / B: 아, 네, 물론이죠.
A: Excuse me, may I squeeze through? / B: Oh, yes, of course.
asking permission to pass in a tight space; polite A/B exchange
통화 좀 하고 올게요. 잠시 실례하겠습니다.
I need to take a call. Please excuse me for a moment.
격식 form 실례하겠습니다 when stepping away from a formal group
nuance: 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor social intrusion — getting a stranger's attention, asking a question, passing by, or entering a space. From Sino-Korean 실례(失禮), literally 'I am committing a breach of etiquette'. It is NOT an apology for a real fault (that requires 죄송합니다) and NOT 'pardon? / say again?' (that is 네? / 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?). Register: 실례합니다 is standard polite; the 격식 form is 실례하겠습니다 / 실례합니다만; clipped 실례 sounds odd in formal contexts and is only murmured casually. The nearest alternatives are 저기요 and 잠시만요/잠깐만요: 저기요 hails a server or stranger casually and is more common in eateries; 잠시만요 means 'one moment / let me through' but can also ask someone to wait. 실례합니다 is the more polished opener before a question or when entering a space. English speakers often misuse it as an all-purpose 'sorry' or as 'pardon?' — neither is correct. In casual restaurants Koreans typically call 저기요, not 실례합니다.

structuredNuance.t: From 실례(失禮), literally 'I am committing a breach of etiquette'. The real use is a polite preface to a minor intrusion — getting attention, asking a question, or passing by. It is not an apology for a real fault.
실례합니다 is standard polite; 실례하겠습니다 / 실례합니다만 are slightly more 격식 (entering a room, stepping away from a meeting). Clipped 실례 sounds awkward in formal settings. You almost never use it in 반말.

Alternatives: 저기요 hails a server or stranger casually and is the default in eateries; 잠시만요/잠깐만요 means 'one moment / let me through' but can also ask someone to wait. 실례합니다 is the more formal, polished opener before a question.
Soften with 저: 저, 실례합니다. Add a clause: 실례지만 (when prefacing an intrusive question). Formal step-away: 잠시 실례하겠습니다. Never say 실례해요 — the verb stem needs either 합니다 or 하겠습니다, not 해요, in this set phrase.

English speakers use 실례합니다 as an all-purpose 'sorry' or 'pardon?' — both are wrong. For fault: 죄송합니다. For 'say again?': 네? / 다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요? Also, using 실례합니다 to hail a waiter at a casual restaurant sounds overly formal — use 저기요 there.

mistakes: Using 실례합니다 as 'sorry' for a real mistake — for fault use 죄송합니다; 실례합니다 is only for a small intrusion.
Saying 실례합니다 to mean 'pardon? / say again?' — to ask for a repeat use 네? or 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Hailing a waiter with 실례합니다 every time — Koreans more often call 저기요 or 여기요 in casual eateries.

english: Excuse me, but… / Pardon me, but…
usage: polite lead-in to a slightly intrusive question
pardon me, may I ask you something
격식, very polite preface to a question
excuse me, but might you happen to…
natural extension; 혹시 softens a personal question
examples: 실례지만, 누구세요?
Excuse me, but who are you?
softening a direct identity question with 실례지만 — without it, 누구세요? sounds blunt
실례지만 나이가 어떻게 되세요?
Pardon me, but how old are you?
prefacing a sensitive personal question; Korean culture expects this cushion
A: 실례지만 길 좀 여쭤봐도 될까요? / B: 네, 말씀하세요.
A: Excuse me, but may I ask for directions? / B: Yes, go ahead.
a courteous full request-exchange to a stranger; note 여쭤보다 (ask, humble form)
nuance: 실례지만 is the polite 'excuse me, but…' you put BEFORE a question that might intrude — asking a stranger's name, age, relationship status, or for directions. It is 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but', meaning 'it's a bit forward of me, but…'. This buffer is not optional small talk — it is culturally expected when your question crosses into personal territory, especially with someone you don't know. Register: 실례지만 is standard polite; 실례하지만 and 실례합니다만 are slightly more 격식; a softer, more casual variant is 실례인데. The nearest alternative is 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), which leans more apologetic and frames asking a favor; the dividing line is that 실례지만 frames a social intrusion ('this question is a bit forward'), while 죄송하지만 frames an imposition ('I'm imposing on you'). Critical grammar rule English speakers miss: 실례지만 must attach to a following clause — it CANNOT end a sentence by itself like English 'excuse me'. To stand alone, say 실례합니다.

structuredNuance.t: 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but' = 'it's a bit forward of me, but…'. The real function is a social cushion that pre-apologizes for an intrusive question, signaling you are aware you might be crossing a line.

실례지만 is standard polite; 실례하지만 / 실례합니다만 are more 격식; 실례인데 is softer and slightly casual. Use any of these before personal questions to a stranger. Never drop the cushion — asking personal questions cold sounds blunt in Korean.

Nearest alternative is 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), which leans apologetic and frames an imposition. The dividing line: 실례지만 = 'this question is a bit forward'; 죄송하지만 = 'I'm imposing on you / asking too much'. They can often swap, but 실례지만 is more about the question's intrusiveness.
Add 혹시 for extra softness: 실례지만 혹시 어디서 일하세요? Use 실례지만 말씀 좀 여쭙겠습니다 as a formal complete opener. In writing, 실례합니다만 is common.

English speakers drop the cushion entirely, firing 나이가 어떻게 되세요? cold — which sounds blunt and rude in Korean. Also, 실례지만 cannot end a sentence alone like English 'excuse me'; it must attach to a following clause. Use 실례합니다 to stand alone.

mistakes: Using 실례지만 alone like English 'excuse me' — it needs a following clause (실례지만, 누구세요?); to stand alone use 실례합니다.
Asking personal questions (age, name, marital status) with no cushion — Korean expects 실례지만/혹시 in front to soften.
Swapping it freely with 죄송하지만 — 실례지만 frames an intrusive question; 죄송하지만 leans toward asking a favor.

english: Thank you for your hard work. / Well done.
usage: thank you for your hard work
polite, to a peer/junior or sideways after work is done
반말, downward to someone younger or a close junior
격식, more respectful acknowledgment of effort
examples: 수고하셨습니다.
Thanks for your hard work.
standard sign-off after a shared task or shift ends
오늘 회의 수고하셨습니다. 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.
Thanks for your work in today's meeting. I'll head out first.
common workplace exit line after a meeting; 먼저 들어가겠습니다 is the polite 'I'm heading out first'
A: 오늘 배송 감사합니다. / B: 수고하셨습니다, 안녕히 계세요.
A: Thanks for the delivery today. / B: Good work, take care.
saying 수고하셨습니다 to a delivery driver; it acknowledges their effort sideways, which is correct
nuance: 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges effort — 'you've worked hard, thank you' — said when a task, shift, meeting, or service is finished. 수고 literally means 'trouble/effort/toil'. It is the standard workplace sign-off and also what you say to a delivery driver or service staff after they've done something for you. The register ladder: 수고했어 (반말, downward) → 수고하셨어요 (softer polite) → 수고하셨습니다 (polite) → 고생 많으셨습니다 / 고생하셨습니다 (warmer, more 격식, stronger emotional weight). The crucial social rule English speakers miss: 수고하세요/수고하셨습니다 is best used SIDEWAYS or DOWNWARD — to peers and juniors. Saying it to a clear superior (your boss, a professor, a much older person) can sound presumptuous, as if you are evaluating their labor from above. To a superior, 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 (used carefully and with sincere tone) is safer. Also critical: 수고하세요 (present) is for someone still working; 수고하셨습니다 (past honorific) is only for when the work is done — mixing tenses is a common error.

structuredNuance.t: 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges effort — 'you've worked hard, thank you' — said when a task, shift, meeting, or service is finished. It is the standard workplace sign-off and what you say to delivery drivers or service staff. 수고 means 'trouble/effort/toil'.

수고했어 (반말, downward to juniors) → 수고하셨어요 (softer polite, peers) → 수고하셨습니다 (standard polite) → 고생 많으셨습니다 (격식, more emotional weight, also safe upward). The directional rule: use 수고하셨습니다 sideways or downward, never up to a boss.

고생 많으셨습니다 is warmer and more emotionally weighted — use it for long, difficult effort (late nights, a tough project). 수고하셨습니다 is the everyday neutral sign-off after any task. 고생 많으셨습니다 also works safely upward when said sincerely.
수고하세요 (present): to someone still working, meaning 'keep up the good work / thanks for your ongoing effort'. 수고하셨습니다 (past): only after work is finished. Never mix them.

Saying 수고하셨습니다 to your boss sounds like you are grading their work from above — it can come off as presumptuous. Use 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 upward instead. Also, do not use 수고하세요 after the work is done — that form is for ongoing work only.

mistakes: Saying 수고하셨습니다 to your boss or a much older superior — it can sound like you're grading them; use 감사합니다 (or 고생 많으셨습니다) instead.
Using 수고했어 with someone older or a stranger — that is 반말; say 수고하셨습니다/수고하셨어요.
Mixing tenses — say 수고하세요 to someone still working, 수고하셨습니다 only after the work is finished.

usage: polite; crediting someone for a good outcome
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, firmer and more neutral
examples: 덕분이에요.
It's thanks to you.
crediting the other person graciously for a good result
A: 잘 지내셨어요? / B: 네, 덕분에 잘 지냈어요.
A: Have you been well? / B: Yes, thanks to you I've been well.
the set polite exchange; 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 is the warm standard reply to 'how have you been?'
이번 일 잘 끝났어요. 다 부장님 덕분입니다.
This project wrapped up well. It's all thanks to you, sir.
격식 form giving a senior full credit; 부장님 덕분 = 'thanks to the department head'
nuance: 덕분에/덕분이에요 credits another person for a POSITIVE result — 'because of you, things went well'. From Sino-Korean 덕분(德分), meaning 'thanks to your virtue/grace/help'. It shines as a gracious, humble gesture toward someone who helped, especially a senior, and is particularly warm in the set exchange 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 in response to 잘 지내셨어요? The register ladder: 덕분이야 (반말) → 덕분이에요/덕분에요 (polite) → 덕분입니다 (격식). The critical contrast English speakers miss is 덕분 vs 때문: 덕분 is for POSITIVE outcomes only ('thanks to'), while 때문 is neutral-to-negative cause ('because of', often implying blame). Saying '너 때문에 잘 됐어' actually sounds sarcastic or odd — credit good things with 덕분에, not 때문에. Also, 덕분에 needs either a result clause following it (덕분에 잘 지냈어요) or the copula 이에요/입니다 to stand as a sentence (덕분이에요/덕분입니다) — you cannot drop these endings and use 덕분에 as a bare English-style shout.

structuredNuance.t: From 덕분(德分), literally 'thanks to your virtue/grace/share'. The real meaning is crediting someone for a POSITIVE outcome — 'because of you, things went well'. It always points to something good happening.

덕분이야 (반말, to friends/juniors) → 덕분이에요/덕분에요 (standard polite) → 덕분입니다 (격식, to seniors or in formal speech). The set phrase 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 is the warm standard polite reply to 잘 지내셨어요?, used across all adult relationships.

Critical contrast: 덕분 is for positive outcomes ('thanks to'); 때문 is neutral-to-negative cause ('because of', often blame). Never say '너 때문에' to credit someone — it implies fault. Use 덕분에 to credit, 때문에 to explain a negative cause.
덕분에 + result clause: 덕분에 잘 됐어요 / 덕분에 합격했어요. Standalone: 덕분이에요 / 다 선생님 덕분입니다. You cannot say bare 덕분에 without a clause or copula following.

Saying '너 때문에' to mean 'thanks to you' sounds like blame or sarcasm — always use 덕분에 for positive credit. Also, 덕분에 cannot stand alone as an exclamation; it needs a result clause (덕분에 잘 됐어요) or the copula (덕분이에요).

mistakes: Saying 너 때문에 for 'thanks to you' — 때문에 sounds like blame; for positive credit use 덕분에.
Replying to '잘 지냈어요?' with bare 덕분 — say the set 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 / 덕분이에요.
Using 덕분 for a bad result ('덕분에 망했어') — that's sarcastic; neutral/negative cause is 때문에.

english: Thank you for your thoughtfulness / for caring.
usage: polite; thanking someone for taking trouble/care
thanks for caring / for the trouble
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식, to a customer/senior, written or spoken
thank you for going to such trouble
examples: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다.
Thank you for your thoughtfulness.
thanking someone who took extra care or attention for you
A: 몸은 좀 어떠세요? / B: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다, 많이 좋아졌어요.
A: How are you feeling? / B: Thank you for asking — I'm much better.
responding warmly to concern about your health; 신경 써 주셔서 thanks the ACT of caring, not just the words
선물까지 챙겨 주시고, 이렇게 신경 써 주셔서 정말 감사합니다.
You even prepared a gift — thank you so much for all your thoughtfulness.
thanking someone who went out of their way; 챙겨 주시다 = 'take care to prepare / look after'
nuance: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 thanks someone for the care, attention, and effort they took on your behalf — for worrying about you, asking after you, or quietly handling something you didn't ask for. 신경(을) 쓰다 literally means 'to put nerves/attention into (something)' — it describes the internal effort of paying attention or worrying, not just a concrete action. The structural engine is the favor pattern ~아/어 주셔서 ('because you kindly did…') + 감사합니다, which frames the care as a gift to you. Register: 신경 써 줘서 고마워 (반말) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 (polite) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다 (격식). The nearest alternative is 도와주셔서 감사합니다 ('thanks for helping'), which thanks a concrete action; the dividing line is that 신경 써 주셔서 specifically thanks the emotional care and ongoing attention, not just a one-time deed. The two English-speaker mistakes: (1) writing 신경써 without a space — the verb is 신경(을) 쓰다, so the gerund is 신경 써; (2) dropping 주다 and saying plain 신경 써서 감사합니다, which removes the 'kindly did for me' nuance and sounds like you are just narrating that they worried.

structuredNuance.t: 신경(을) 쓰다 literally means 'to put one's nerves/attention into (something)' — i.e. 'to worry, to take pains over, to fret'. The full phrase thanks someone for that internal effort and ongoing care they showed toward you.

신경 써 줘서 고마워 (반말) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 (polite) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다 (격식). Use this when someone showed sustained concern — asking after your health, remembering something important to you, or quietly managing something.

Nearest alternative: 도와주셔서 감사합니다 ('thanks for helping'), which thanks a concrete action. The dividing line: 신경 써 주셔서 thanks emotional care and ongoing attention; 도와주셔서 thanks a specific deed. Use 신경 써 주셔서 when the effort was internal/sustained.
Add 이렇게 or 이렇게까지 to stress the extent: 이렇게 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다. Swap 감사합니다 for 감사드립니다 upward: 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다.

Two errors: (1) Writing 신경써 without a space — the verb is 신경(을) 쓰다, so the spacing is 신경 써. (2) Dropping 주다 and saying '신경 써서 감사합니다' — without ~아/어 주셔서 you lose the 'kindly did me a favor' nuance and it sounds like you're just describing their worry.

mistakes: Dropping 주다 → '신경 써서 감사합니다' — without ~아/어 주셔서 it loses the 'kindly did me a favor' nuance; keep 신경 써 주셔서.
Writing 신경써 with no space — the verb is 신경(을) 쓰다, so it is 신경 써 (주셔서).
Using it to a close friend in full 존댓말 — too stiff; say 신경 써 줘서 고마워.

english: Excuse me! (to get attention) / Over here!
usage: the everyday polite way to flag a stranger or call a server
calling staff to YOUR table; signaling your spot
반말-ish, soft opener to a friend or to trail into a question
we'd like to order over here
natural extension; flagging staff to take an order
examples: 저기요, 이거 얼마예요?
Excuse me, how much is this?
flagging a shop clerk to ask a question; 저기요 comes first, then the question
A: 여기요, 물 좀 주세요. / B: 네, 잠시만요.
A: Excuse me (over here), some water please. / B: Yes, one moment.
calling a server to your table; 여기요 signals YOUR location, not theirs
저기요, 이거 떨어뜨리셨어요.
Excuse me, you dropped this.
getting a passing stranger's attention to help them; natural and polite
nuance: 저기요 is the workhorse 'excuse me' for HAILING someone — a server, a shop clerk, or a stranger you need to flag down — and it is far more common in daily life than the textbook 실례합니다. The word breaks down as 저기 ('over there', a distal deictic pointing to the listener's space) + 요 (the polite sentence-final particle), so it literally means 'hey, over there'. 여기요 ('over here') flips the direction: it calls staff to YOUR location. Both are polite-but-casual: perfectly normal in shops, cafés, and restaurants, but a touch direct toward a clear senior or in a very formal setting, where 실례합니다 / 실례지만 is more polished. Register: bare 저기 is the soft 반말-ish opener to someone you know ('저기, 있잖아…'); 저기요/여기요 add 요 for strangers and staff. The dividing line versus 실례합니다: 저기요/여기요 get attention quickly and are the real-life default in eateries; 실례합니다 is more formal and covers not just hailing but also passing by or interrupting. English speakers err in two ways: over-using the formal 실례합니다 everywhere (sounds stiff in a café), or trying to hail a server with 미안해요 ('I'm sorry for a fault') or by snapping fingers — both are culturally off.

structuredNuance.t: 저기 is a distal deictic — 'over there (where you are)' — and 요 makes it politely sentence-final. Literally: 'hey, over there!' The real use is hailing someone: a server, a clerk, a stranger. 여기요 ('here!') is the same structure pointing to the SPEAKER'S location instead.

저기 (반말-ish, friends) → 저기요/여기요 (polite everyday, strangers/staff) → 실례합니다 (more formal, or when passing/interrupting). 저기요/여기요 are the default in cafés, restaurants, and shops — comfortable and direct, not rude.

The dividing line versus 실례합니다: 저기요/여기요 quickly get attention and are the daily default in eateries; 실례합니다 is more polished and formal, and also covers passing by or interrupting a conversation. Both are correct; the choice is about register.

여기요 + request: 여기요, 물 한 잔만요 / 여기요, 주문할게요. 저기요 + question: 저기요, 여기 주차 가능한가요? Soften: 저기요, 잠깐만요. Do NOT use 저기요 alone as a farewell or general filler — it strictly serves to hail someone present. Also, 저기요? with a questioning rise can politely mean 'yes?' when someone calls your name.

Two common errors: over-using 실례합니다 in casual eateries (sounds stiff); and using 미안해요 to hail a waiter (it means 'I'm sorry for a fault', not a hail). In Korea, calling out 저기요 clearly is natural and expected — do not be timid about it.

mistakes: Using 실례합니다 to call a waiter every time — in casual eateries Koreans say 저기요 or 여기요; 실례합니다 sounds overly formal there.
Saying 미안해요 to get a stranger's or server's attention — that's 'I'm sorry (for a fault)', not a hail; use 저기요.
Confusing 저기요 (hailing) with 거기요 — to flag someone it's 저기요/여기요; 거기 ('there, by you') isn't the attention-getter.

english: I ask for your understanding. / Please bear with us.
usage: 격식 polite; announcements, notices, to customers
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
we ask that you kindly understand (very formal)
natural extension; 너른/넓은 양해 = generous understanding
examples: 공사로 인해 소음이 있을 수 있으니 양해 부탁드립니다.
There may be noise due to construction, so we ask for your understanding.
a typical posted or announced public notice — institutional register
배송이 다소 지연되고 있습니다. 고객님들의 너른 양해 부탁드립니다.
Shipping is somewhat delayed. We ask for our customers' kind understanding.
a business apologizing formally for a delay; 너른 양해 = generous/gracious understanding
A: 시스템 점검으로 서비스가 잠시 중단됩니다. 양해 부탁드립니다. / B: 네, 알겠습니다.
A: The service will be briefly suspended for system maintenance. We ask for your understanding. / B: Understood.
intercom or notice context; shows this phrase is used to ANNOUNCE, not to apologize one-on-one
nuance: 양해 부탁드립니다 is formal, institutional 'please understand / bear with us' — used when an organization asks its customers, passengers, or audience to tolerate an inconvenience (delay, noise, closure, policy change). 양해(諒解) is Sino-Korean for 'making allowances / granting understanding'; 부탁드리다 is the humble form of 부탁하다 ('to request'), literally 'I respectfully offer this request upward'. This is announcement and customer-service language: signs, intercom messages, emails, formal business notices. It is inherently 격식. The still-more-formal variant is 양해해 주시기 바랍니다 (written notices, official broadcasts); casually to a friend you shrink it to 이해해 줘 / 양해 좀 해 줘. The dividing line versus 이해해 주세요: 이해해 주세요 is warm and personal, one-to-one; 양해 부탁드립니다 is institutional, addressing a group. Using it in casual one-on-one conversation sounds like you are reading from a corporate notice board. English speakers also mishandle 부탁: in this phrase it pairs with the humble 드리다 (부탁드립니다), not the plain 합니다 (부탁합니다) — mixing them is a register error upward.

structuredNuance.t: 양해(諒解) = 'making allowances / granting understanding'; 부탁드리다 = 'I respectfully request (upward)'. Together: 'We humbly ask that you make allowances for this situation.' The real use is institutional: asking customers or the public to tolerate inconvenience.
Inherently 격식 and institutional. For one-on-one personal use: 이해해 줘 / 양해 좀 해 줘 (반말) → 이해해 주세요 / 양해해 주세요 (personal polite). Reserve 양해 부탁드립니다 for notices, announcements, and customer communications.

Nearest everyday alternative: 이해해 주세요 ('please understand'), which is warm and personal, one-to-one. The dividing line: 양해 부탁드립니다 addresses a group from an institution; 이해해 주세요 is personal empathy. Using 양해 부탁드립니다 in personal chat sounds like a corporate bot.
너른/넓은 양해 부탁드립니다 (begging generous understanding), 양해해 주시기 바랍니다 (very formal written), 고객님의 양해를 구합니다 (also formal). To humanize in a business email: 불편을 드려 정말 죄송합니다 (apology) + 양해 부탁드립니다 (request).

Using 양해 부탁드립니다 in casual one-on-one conversation sounds like a corporate announcement — use 이해해 줘 or 이해해 주세요 instead. Also, 부탁 pairs with the humble 드리다 (부탁드립니다) upward, not 합니다 (부탁합니다) — mixing them is a register error.

mistakes: Using 양해 부탁드립니다 in casual one-on-one talk — it sounds like a corporate notice; with a friend say 이해해 줘 / 양해 좀 해 줘.
Confusing 양해 (making allowances for inconvenience) with plain 이해 (understanding a fact) — for tolerating trouble use 양해.
Saying 양해 부탁한다 to someone senior — use the humble 부탁드립니다, not 부탁한다/부탁해.

english: Excuse me for a second. / Let me just slip in for a moment.
usage: polite; before passing, reaching past, or briefly intruding
반말-ish/clipped, among close people or muttered
please excuse me for a moment (formal)
격식, before stepping away or entering
just one quick second, excuse me
examples: 잠깐 실례할게요, 여기 좀 지나갈게요.
Excuse me a sec, let me get through here.
squeezing past in a tight aisle; both the excuse and the intent are stated
A: 잠깐 실례할게요, 이 자리 잠깐 비켜 주실 수 있을까요? / B: 아, 네 물론이죠.
A: Excuse me for a moment, could you step aside briefly? / B: Oh, sure, of course.
politely asking someone to move, with their consent — both the excuse and the request
통화 좀 하고 올게요. 잠시 실례하겠습니다.
I need to take a call. Please excuse me for a moment.
격식 form 실례하겠습니다 when stepping away from a formal meeting or group
nuance: 잠깐 실례할게요 is a brief, courteous heads-up before you reach past someone, slip by, step away, or briefly intrude on a space or group. 잠깐/잠시 means 'for a short while', 실례하다 means 'commit a small breach of etiquette', and ~ㄹ게요 is the 'I'm going to…' announcement form that flags YOUR own imminent action rather than ordering anyone else. The formality ladder: clipped 잠깐 실례 (casual) → 잠깐 실례할게요 (polite) → 잠시 실례하겠습니다 (격식). The ~ㄹ게요 vs ~겠습니다 split mirrors formality: use ~겠습니다 in formal/professional settings. The nearest alternatives are 잠시만요 / 잠깐만요 ('one moment / let me through'), which are shorter and very common in daily life, and bare 실례합니다 (a touch more formal). The dividing line: 잠깐 실례할게요 explicitly announces a brief, self-initiated intrusion; 잠시만요 is more versatile but can also mean 'hold on / wait'. Two English-speaker mistakes: (1) using ~ㄹ게요 toward a senior in formal settings where ~겠습니다 is safer; (2) saying 잠깐 실례하세요 — the 하세요 form commands the OTHER person to excuse themselves, but you mean YOURSELF, so it must be 실례할게요/실례하겠습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 잠깐 = 'for a short while'; 실례하다 = 'commit a small breach of etiquette'; ~ㄹ게요 = 'I'm going to (announcing own action)'. Together: 'I'm going to commit a small intrusion for just a moment.' The ~ㄹ게요 ending is key — it announces YOUR action, not a command to them.
Clipped 잠깐 실례 (casual/muttered) → 잠깐 실례할게요 (polite) → 잠시 실례하겠습니다 (격식). The ~ㄹ게요 vs ~겠습니다 split tracks formality directly: use ~겠습니다 in professional or senior-present contexts.

Alternatives: 잠시만요 / 잠깐만요 ('one moment / let me through') — shorter and very common, but also means 'hold on / wait'. 잠깐 실례할게요 more explicitly flags a brief self-initiated intrusion. In tight spaces, either works.

Add 잠깐만 to stress brevity: 잠깐만 실례할게요. Formal step-away: 잠시 실례하겠습니다. Add reason after: 잠깐 실례할게요, 전화 받고 올게요. The clipped 잠깐 실례 is muttered while passing and socially acceptable in casual settings, but use the full form with anyone you don't know well.

Two mistakes: (1) Saying 잠깐 실례하세요 — 하세요 commands THE OTHER PERSON to excuse themselves; you want to excuse YOURSELF, so say 실례할게요/실례하겠습니다. (2) Using ~ㄹ게요 to a clear superior in a formal setting — prefer the more deferential 잠시 실례하겠습니다.

mistakes: Saying 잠깐 실례하세요 — 하세요 tells the other person to excuse themselves; for your own action say 실례할게요/실례하겠습니다.
Using ~ㄹ게요 to a clear superior in a formal setting — prefer 잠시 실례하겠습니다.
Forgetting Koreans more often just say 잠시만요/잠깐만요 to pass or pause — it's the most natural everyday form.

english: Are you okay? / Is everything all right?
usage: 존댓말; checking on someone who stumbled, looks unwell, etc.
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식, e.g. staff to a customer or a senior
natural extension; 혹시 softens the check-in
examples: A: 어, 괜찮으세요? 많이 놀라셨죠. / B: 네, 괜찮아요. 감사합니다.
A: Oh, are you okay? That must have startled you. / B: Yes, I'm all right. Thank you.
the natural A/B exchange right after someone gets a shock or stumbles — notice the natural pair of 죄송합니다 + 괜찮으세요?
안색이 안 좋아 보이는데, 괜찮으세요? 좀 쉬실래요?
You look pale — are you all right? Want to rest a bit?
a caring full check-in on someone unwell; 안색이 안 좋다 = 'your color looks off'
넘어지셨는데, 괜찮으세요? 다치신 데 없으세요?
You fell — are you okay? Are you hurt anywhere?
checking for injury after a fall; 다치신 데 없으세요? = 'are you hurt anywhere?' is the natural follow-up
nuance: 괜찮으세요? is the polite 'are you okay?' used to check on someone who tripped, got startled, looks unwell, or had a hard time. The 으시 honorific infix raises the LISTENER, making it respectful to anyone you'd use 존댓말 with. Register: 괜찮아? (반말) → 괜찮으세요? (polite) → 괜찮으십니까? (격식/서비스). When you bump into someone or they stumble, Koreans immediately pair 죄송합니다 + 괜찮으세요? — this pairing is a cultural reflex worth memorizing. The nearest alternative is 어디 안 좋으세요? ('is something wrong / are you unwell?'), which specifically targets physical illness; 괜찮으세요? is broader, covering shock, distress, injury, and wellness. Critical distinction English speakers miss: 괜찮아요 (statement, falling tone) means 'I'm fine / no thanks'; 괜찮으세요? (question, rising tone + 으세요 ending) asks about the OTHER person — the form and intonation are different. A second error is saying 괜찮아? to a stranger or elder — that is 반말 and sounds rude.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮으세요? is the polite question form of 괜찮다, used to check on someone who tripped, was shocked, or looks unwell. When you bump into someone, the culturally expected reflex is 죄송합니다 + 괜찮으세요? together.
괜찮아? (반말, friends/juniors) → 괜찮으세요? (polite) → 괜찮으십니까? (격식, staff to customer). The 으시 honorific infix raises the listener. Always use 괜찮으세요? with strangers and seniors.

Nearest alternative: 어디 안 좋으세요? ('is something wrong / are you unwell?') — targets physical illness specifically. 괜찮으세요? is broader (shock, distress, injury, wellness all covered). Use 어디 안 좋으세요? when someone looks persistently ill.
Follow up naturally: 괜찮으세요? + 다치신 데 없으세요? (any injuries?), 괜찮으세요? + 좀 쉬실래요? (want to rest?). Soften with 혹시: 혹시 괜찮으세요?

English speakers confuse 괜찮아요 (statement: 'I'm fine / no thanks') with 괜찮으세요? (question about them) — the 으세요 ending and rising tone make it a question about the OTHER person. Also, saying 괜찮아? to a stranger is 반말 and rude; always use 괜찮으세요? with people you are not close with.

mistakes: Asking 괜찮아? to a stranger or senior — that's 반말; use 괜찮으세요?/괜찮으십니까?.
Confusing the offer-decline 괜찮아요 with the check-in 괜찮으세요? — the 으세요 + rising tone makes it a question about THEM.
Saying 괜찮해요/괜찮하세요 — there's no ㅎ; the stem is 괜찮다 → 괜찮아요, 괜찮으세요.

english: I'd like to ask a favor. / Please (I'm counting on you).
usage: humble polite; making a request of a senior/customer
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
I look forward to working with you / please take care of this
격식, first meetings, handing off a task
may I ask you a small favor
examples: 이 자료 검토 좀 부탁드립니다.
Could I ask you to review this document, please?
asking a colleague or senior for a task; 부탁드립니다 frames it as a humble request, not a command
처음 뵙겠습니다. 앞으로 잘 부탁드립니다.
Nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.
the indispensable first-meeting set line; 잘 부탁드립니다 is a goodwill formula, NOT a comment on quality
A: 이번 건 제가 담당하게 됐습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다. / B: 저야말로요, 잘 부탁드립니다.
A: I'll be in charge of this matter. I'm counting on your support. / B: Likewise, looking forward to working together.
reciprocal 잘 부탁드립니다 exchange — this back-and-forth is extremely common in Korean professional and social contexts
nuance: 부탁드립니다 is the humble, polite way to ask a favor or entrust a task — literally 'I respectfully offer this request upward to you'. The base is 부탁(을) 하다 ('to make a request'), raised to the humble 부탁(을) 드리다 by replacing 하다 with 드리다 (the humble auxiliary 'give upward'). The set phrase 잘 부탁드립니다 is indispensable in Korean life: it greases first meetings ('please be good to me / I look forward to working with you') and task hand-offs ('please handle this well') and is said reciprocally. Register: 부탁해 (반말) → 부탁해요 (polite) → 부탁드립니다 (humble/격식). The dividing line versus a bare imperative like ~해 주세요 ('please do it') is deference and softness: 부탁드립니다 frames the whole thing as a humble plea, which is the expected tone when asking upward. Two English-speaker mistakes: (1) using plain 부탁합니다 or 부탁해 toward a senior — use the humble 부탁드립니다; (2) interpreting 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'please do a good job' — it is a fixed social formula of goodwill and mutual reliance, not performance feedback.

structuredNuance.t: 부탁(을) 드리다 = 'I respectfully offer/give this request upward'. The 드리다 (humble 'give upward') is what makes it deferential. The real meaning is a humble, polite plea — much softer than a direct command ~해 주세요.
부탁해 (반말) → 부탁해요 (polite) → 부탁드립니다 (humble/격식). Use 부탁드립니다 with seniors, customers, and anyone you need to address deferentially. 잘 부탁드립니다 is obligatory at first meetings and task hand-offs.
The dividing line versus ~해 주세요 ('please do it') is deference: ~해 주세요 is a polite request; 부탁드립니다 is a humble plea. When asking upward, 부탁드립니다 is far more deferential and expected.
부탁 좀 드릴게요 (softer, 'may I ask a small favor'). 잘 부탁드립니다 (set first-meeting/hand-off formula). ~를 부탁드립니다 (task-specific: 이 자료 검토를 부탁드립니다). Adding 다시 한번: 다시 한번 잘 부탁드립니다.

Two traps: (1) Using 부탁합니다 or 부탁해 toward a senior — the humble 드리다 (부탁드립니다) is required. (2) Reading 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'do a good job' — it is a fixed social formula of goodwill and mutual reliance at a new relationship's start, never performance feedback.

mistakes: Saying 부탁해 or 부탁한다 to a senior/customer — use the humble 부탁드립니다.
Reading 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'do a good job' — it's a set goodwill phrase for first meetings/hand-offs.
Issuing a bare command (해 주세요) where deference is needed — soften with 부탁드립니다 to sound properly polite upward.
